meta.subtitle: Chemicals cycle turning: Q2'26 swung to profit on price, but the dividend leans on negative free cash flow

analystCommentary:
Dow enters the second half of 2026 with the chemicals cycle turning up rather than down. Second-quarter net sales were $12.1 billion, up 20% year-over-year, and the quarter swung to GAAP net income of $802 million from a loss of $801 million a year earlier. GAAP EPS was $0.99 and operating EPS was $1.44, against an operating loss of $0.42 per share in the year-ago quarter. Operating EBIT of $1.6 billion improved $1.7 billion year-over-year, driven mostly by higher prices while volume fell 1%. That distinction matters: the recovery so far is price-led, not volume-led.

We rate DOW HOLD with a target range of $29 to $39, bracketing our $34 base case. The base case sits close to the Street's $34.44 consensus target but below it, reflecting cyclical risk we think consensus underweights. The bull case ($41) assumes Transform to Outperform delivers its $2 billion Operating EBITDA target while polyethylene pricing holds. The bear case ($22, about 23% below the $28.65 price) assumes pricing normalizes and the cycle relapses toward the FY25 loss.

Two facts keep us at HOLD rather than BUY. First, consensus expects FY27E EPS of $1.78, below FY26E of $2.39 - the Street itself models a give-back. Second, the dividend still ran ahead of free cash flow in FY25, so the 4.96% yield rests on a cash flow that has not yet recovered. The recovery is real; it is not yet proven through a full cycle.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Dow Inc. is a materials science company headquartered in Midland, Michigan and founded in 1897. It makes ethylene, propylene, polyethylene and other plastics and chemical intermediates for packaging, infrastructure, mobility and consumer applications, selling across the United States, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, India, the Asia Pacific and Latin America. The company runs three operating segments: Packaging & Specialty Plastics, Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure, and Performance Materials & Coatings. Packaging & Specialty Plastics supplies ethylene, propylene, polyethylene, aromatics and ethylene derivatives such as polyolefin elastomers. Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure covers polyurethanes, chlor-alkali and vinyl, and construction chemicals. Performance Materials & Coatings provides architectural and industrial coatings, silicon metals and siloxanes. Dow reported sales of approximately $40 billion in 2025 and operates manufacturing sites in 29 countries. It employed about 34,600 people at year-end 2025, falling to approximately 32,800 at June 30, 2026 as restructuring progressed. This is a cyclical, commodity-heavy business: FY25 revenue of $40.0 billion was down 7.0% year-over-year, and the year produced an operating loss.

thesis.body: Dow is a cyclical commodity-chemicals producer coming off a trough. FY25 revenue fell to $40.0 billion, {- down 7.0% -}, gross margin compressed to 6.3%, and the company posted a net loss of $2.6 billion (-$3.70 diluted EPS). The second quarter of 2026 marks an inflection: net sales rose {+ 20% +} to $12.1 billion, GAAP EPS was $0.99, and operating EBITDA reached $2,312 million versus $703 million a year earlier. The turn is driven by price rather than volume, which fell 1%, and by self-help, with management now guiding to more than $1.3 billion of in-year benefits. The bull path is that Transform to Outperform delivers its $2 billion Operating EBITDA target and pricing holds. The bear path is that pricing normalizes on soft volume and the cycle relapses. With consensus FY27E EPS ($1.78) already below FY26E ($2.39) and the dividend running ahead of free cash flow, we see the risk-reward as balanced and rate the shares HOLD.

catalysts: Transform to Outperform, Dow's self-help and cost program, is the main near-term earnings lever, and management lifted its in-year benefit guidance alongside Q2'26 results.
Polyethylene price recovery is lifting Packaging & Specialty Plastics: local price rose 30% year-over-year in Q2'26, driving a sharp swing in segment Operating EBIT.
Structural demand pockets could support volume: Industrial Solutions cited alkoxylation investments and data center applications, and Consumer Solutions saw downstream silicones growth.
Cash inflows beyond operations: Dow received a Canada Revenue Agency refund of approximately $318 million (US) in July 2026 tied to the Nova matter.
risks: The recovery is price-led: Q2'26 sales growth came from higher prices, not volume, so a reversal in commodity prices would pull revenue back down.
Dividend cover is thin: FY25 free cash flow did not cover the dividend, and buybacks are suspended.
Cyclicality is severe: FY25 was a full-year net loss, and one strong quarter does not undo it.
Geopolitical exposure: portions of Dow's Middle East joint ventures have been directly impacted by the regional conflict, with feedstock logistics through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The multi-year income statement shows a deep cyclical downtrend into FY25 and an inflection in Q2'26. Revenue fell from $56.9 billion in FY22 to $40.0 billion in FY25, a {- 7.0% -} decline in FY25 alone. Gross margin compressed from 19.6% in FY21 to 6.3% in FY25, operating income turned to {- -$2.7 billion -} (operating margin -6.6%), and net income was {- -$2.6 billion -} (-$3.70 diluted EPS). EBITDA collapsed to $0.2 billion in FY25 from $11.0 billion in FY21.

Q2'26 broke the trend. Net sales rose {+ 20% +} to $12.1 billion, and the quarter's operating margin was about 6.2%. Cost of sales fell to 82.1% of net sales from 94.2% a year earlier, the clearest sign of margin recovery. GAAP net income was $802 million versus a loss of $801 million, operating EBIT improved {+ $1.7 billion +} year-over-year to $1.6 billion, and operating EBITDA rose to $2,312 million from $703 million. By segment, Packaging & Specialty Plastics Operating EBIT reached $1,278 million (from $71 million) and Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure returned to $246 million of Operating EBIT (from -$185 million), while Performance Materials & Coatings slipped to $133 million (from $152 million) on higher fixed and turnaround costs. Restructuring and asset-related charges were $503 million in the quarter. Trailing-twelve-month operating margin remained negative at -3.0%, a reminder that a single strong quarter has not yet repaired the full-year picture.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Dow's balance sheet is adequate, but the vendor data thin out after FY23. Total equity was $17.5 billion at FY25, down from $21.2 billion at FY22. Cash and short-term investments were $3.8 billion at FY25, up from $2.2 billion at FY24. The current ratio was 1.97 at FY25 and 1.75 on a trailing-twelve-month basis, so near-term liquidity looks sound.

The gap is leverage. The data source reports total debt of $0.1 billion and net debt of -$2.9 billion at FY23 but leaves FY24 and FY25 total debt and net debt blank, so we cannot state a current net-debt or net-debt/EBITDA figure from this pack. Interest coverage and EV/EBITDA are likewise not available. Investors relying on this report should treat leverage as unquantified here rather than low; the FY23 figures predate FY24 and FY25, years of weak-to-negative free cash flow and, in FY25, a net loss that would have drawn on the balance sheet. A 10-K risk factor flags that a downgrade below investment grade would raise borrowing costs and reduce liquidity, which underlines why the missing leverage data matter.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation deteriorated through the downturn and is only now turning. Operating cash flow fell from $7.5 billion in FY22 to $1.0 billion in FY25. Capital expenditure was -$2.5 billion in FY25, so free cash flow was {- -$1.4 billion -} (an FCF margin of -3.6%), following roughly breakeven free cash flow in FY24. Against that, the company paid $1.5 billion of dividends in FY25 and suspended buybacks (FY25 repurchases $0.00). Paying a dividend larger than free cash flow in a loss-making year is the central capital-allocation tension in this report.

The quarter offers some relief. Cash provided by operating activities was $1,324 million in Q2'26, up $1,794 million year-over-year from -$470 million, driven by higher earnings. Dividends in the quarter were $253 million. If operating cash flow sustains the Q2'26 pace, free cash flow can turn positive and the dividend becomes easier to defend; if not, the payout stays under scrutiny. That capital expenditure was up from -$1.5 billion in FY21, reflecting investment through the trough, including the Alberta net-zero cracker.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
Standard earnings multiples are not meaningful at the trough. Trailing P/E is -15.7x because the last twelve months were loss-making, and EV/EBITDA is not available in this pack. Price-to-sales is 0.5x, consistent with a low-margin commodity producer. The forward picture is the useful one: on FY26E EPS of $2.39 the shares trade at about 12.0x (next-twelve-month forward P/E), but on FY27E EPS of $1.78 the multiple rises to roughly 16.1x, because consensus expects earnings to give back ground in FY27. The gap between those two multiples is the valuation debate in one line: pay 12x for a recovering FY26, or 16x for an FY27 the Street already marks lower.

Consensus target is $34.44, a 20.2% premium to the $28.65 price, with a median of $34.00 and a range of $29.00 to $41.00. Nineteen analysts split six Buy, twelve Hold and one Sell - a Buy consensus in name but a Hold consensus in weight. Our own target range of $29 to $39 sits inside the Street range and brackets our $34 base case.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Transform to Outperform delivers its full $2 billion Operating EBITDA target and polyethylene pricing holds; earnings recover toward mid-cycle and the shares approach the top of the analyst range ($41.00) and the prior 52-week high of $42.74.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The recovery holds but moderates: FY26E revenue near $43.6 billion and EPS of $2.39, with FY27E EPS easing to $1.78 as pricing normalizes; fair value near the $34.00 median analyst target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Pricing normalizes on soft volume (Q2'26 volume down 1%, Asia Pacific down 9%) and the cycle relapses toward the FY25 loss; the shares retest toward the 52-week low of $20.65, with our $22 bear case about 23% below the $28.65 price.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bear at 30% and the Bull at 25%. The heavy Bear weight reflects two things: the recovery is price-led with volume down 1% in Q2'26, and consensus itself models an FY27 earnings give-back. The Base case anchors on the median analyst target and consensus FY26E revenue of $43.6 billion. The Bull case requires the full $2 billion of Transform to Outperform benefits to land and pricing to hold; the Bear case is a real relapse toward the FY25 loss and the $20.65 low, not a formality, with our Bear implied price of $22 about 23% below the current price. On these weights the probability-weighted value sits modestly above today's price but short of the Street target, which is why we rate the shares HOLD rather than BUY: the expected upside is real but the reward does not clearly outweigh the cyclical downside.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Dow reports in a single reportable segment in this data pack, but it operates three businesses: Packaging & Specialty Plastics, Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure, and Performance Materials & Coatings. In Q2'26 the recovery was led by Packaging & Specialty Plastics, where higher polyethylene prices lifted Operating EBIT sharply; Industrial Intermediates & Infrastructure swung back to positive Operating EBIT, helped by the suspension of Sadara equity losses; and Performance Materials & Coatings lagged as higher fixed and turnaround costs offset self-help. The common thread is that the businesses rise and fall with the commodity chemicals cycle rather than on company-specific pricing power.

moatFactors.name: Scale and asset integration
moatFactors.body: Dow operates manufacturing sites in 29 countries with roughly $40 billion of annual sales and an integrated ethylene-to-derivatives value chain. Integration and scale lower unit costs and let the company flex feedstocks, a genuine structural advantage. They do not confer pricing power: products are largely commodities and margins are set by the cycle, as the 6.3% FY25 gross margin shows.

moatFactors.name: Feedstock cost position
moatFactors.body: The company operates in cost-advantaged regions, including the U.S. & Canada and Latin America, and says feedstock flexibility let it run its European assets competitively through a volatile energy environment. This is a durable cost edge, but it is a cost edge, not a demand or price edge.

moatFactors.name: Pricing power
moatFactors.body: Prices are set by global supply and demand for commodity chemicals. Q2'26 local price rose 20% because the cycle turned, not because Dow controls price; the same mechanism drove the FY25 collapse to an operating loss. Through-cycle returns are volatile and turned negative in FY25.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs
moatFactors.body: For commodity grades of polyethylene, polyurethanes and chlor-alkali, customers can source from multiple global suppliers. Specialty and downstream silicones and coatings carry more differentiation, but they are the smaller part of the mix.

businessMoat.durability: Dow's advantages are real but narrow. Scale, integration and low-cost feedstock positions give it a structural cost advantage that persists across the cycle, which is why we assign a narrow rather than no moat. What the advantages cannot do is stabilize returns: gross margin fell from 19.6% in FY21 to the mid-single digits by FY25, operating income turned negative, and full-year 2025 was a net loss. A cost advantage in a commodity business narrows losses at the trough and widens gains at the peak, but it does not remove the cycle. The Alberta net-zero cracker and continued investment aim to extend the cost position into the next cycle, while Transform to Outperform targets a leaner cost base. The durability question is therefore not whether the cost edge survives - it likely does - but whether demand and pricing recover enough to make that edge earn an adequate return on capital. On the evidence in this filing, that recovery has begun but is not yet proven.

points: Cyclical rebound: Q2'26 net sales rose 20% year-over-year to $12.1 billion, with increases in all three segments and all geographic regions; consensus FY26E revenue is about $43.6 billion, up 9%.
The rebound is price-led, not volume-led: the Q2'26 gain came almost entirely from higher prices while volume fell 1%, so the durability of growth depends on whether pricing holds.

Self-help is the near-term earnings lever: Transform to Outperform targets at least $2 billion of Operating EBITDA improvement and management guides to more than $1.3 billion of in-year benefits, though only $190 million was delivered in H1'26.

Structural demand pockets: Industrial Solutions cited alkoxylation investments and data center applications, and Consumer Solutions saw downstream silicones growth in consumer, electronics and home care.
Consensus expects the rebound to fade: FY27E revenue of $42.9 billion is slightly below FY26E, and FY27E EPS of $1.78 is below FY26E of $2.39.

management.leadership: Leadership changed at the top mid-2026. On April 14, 2026, the Board appointed Karen S. Carter as Chief Executive Officer effective July 1, 2026; she succeeded Jim Fitterling, who moved from CEO to Executive Chair, and she also joined the Board effective July 1, 2026. The second-quarter results, reported in July under Carter, showed operating EPS of $1.44 against a $0.42 loss a year earlier, and she raised expected in-year self-help benefits to more than $1.3 billion. Headcount fell from about 34,600 at year-end 2025 to roughly 32,800 at June 30, 2026, consistent with the restructuring underway. The transition is recent, so management's execution on Transform to Outperform through the back half of 2026 is the main thing to watch.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is the tension in this report. In FY25 the company paid a dividend that exceeded its free cash flow and repurchased no stock (FY25 repurchases $0.00), so the payout ran ahead of internally generated cash. Capital expenditure was -$2.5 billion in FY25, up from -$1.5 billion in FY21, as Dow invested through the trough, including the Alberta net-zero cracker. The Board declared a $0.35 per share dividend in April 2026 - the 459th consecutive dividend since 1912 - and paid $253 million in Q2'26. Management frames balanced capital allocation as a priority and has monetized assets, selling interests in Diamond Infrastructure Solutions to a Macquarie-managed fund (40% in Q2'25, a further 9% in Q3'25). The dividend's defensibility now hinges on the cash-flow recovery that Q2'26 began, when operating cash flow turned sharply positive year-over-year.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A proxy statement filed February 27, 2026. The Board determined that eleven director nominees are independent - Samuel R. Allen, Gaurdie E. Banister Jr., Wesley G. Bush, Richard K. Davis, Jerri DeVard, Debra L. Dial, Jeff M. Fettig, Jacqueline C. Hinman, Luis Alberto Moreno, Jill S. Wyant and Daniel W. Yohannes - a substantial majority of the Board. At the proxy date, Mr. Fitterling, then Chair and CEO, was the non-independent member; all members of the Audit, Compensation and Leadership Development, Corporate Governance, and Environment, Health, Safety & Technology committees are independent. The Board does not require the Chair and CEO roles to be combined or separated, deciding annually; the July 2026 split of CEO (Carter) from Executive Chair (Fitterling) is consistent with that flexibility. Related-person transactions are reviewed and approved by the Corporate Governance Committee under written policies. At the April 9, 2026 annual meeting, all incumbent directors were re-elected.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt in this pack covers board independence, leadership structure and related-person transaction policy, but does not include the beneficial-ownership tables, so we do not quote an insider or 5%-holder ownership figure. Related-person transactions are governed by a written policy administered by the Corporate Governance Committee, which weighs commercial reasonableness, materiality and conflicts of interest before approving any transaction.

idiosyncratic: Dividend sustainability. The 4.96% yield rests on a recovery in cash flow that has only just begun; in FY25 the dividend exceeded free cash flow and the company repurchased no stock. If operating cash flow does not sustain the improved Q2'26 pace, the payout stays under scrutiny.

Price-led recovery. Q2'26 revenue growth was almost entirely price: local price rose 20% while volume fell 1%, with Asia Pacific volume down 9% and EMEAI down 4%. Commodity prices can reverse quickly, and consensus already models FY27E EPS ($1.78) below FY26E ($2.39).

Execution on Transform to Outperform. The program targets at least $2 billion of Operating EBITDA improvement, but only $190 million was delivered in H1'26; the guided $1.3 billion-plus of in-year benefits is not yet in the run-rate.

Limited leverage visibility. The data pack reports total and net debt only through FY23 (total debt $0.1 billion, net debt -$2.9 billion) and leaves FY24-FY25 blank, so current leverage and net-debt/EBITDA cannot be verified from this report after a loss-making FY25 and two years of negative free cash flow.

Joint-venture stress. Q2'26 equity results improved partly because Dow suspended recognizing its share of Sadara joint-venture losses, and Middle East joint ventures have been directly impacted by the regional conflict.
risks.systemic: Dow is exposed to the global chemicals cycle and macro conditions it does not control. The 10-K risk factors note that increased competition has produced lower prices and lower sales volume and that these pressures may worsen in the near term. Energy and feedstock price volatility is a persistent input risk. The Middle East conflict and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have affected feedstock supply chains, raised transportation and operating costs, and hit Dow's regional joint ventures. Trade policy is a further overhang: the 10-K notes that new U.S. tariffs have pushed the average tariff rate to levels not seen since the 1930s, which can lower sales volume. Access to credit and any downgrade below investment grade would raise borrowing costs. Finally, climate-related transition costs and the execution risk of large decarbonization projects such as the Alberta net-zero cracker sit on the long-term horizon.

body: We rate Dow HOLD with a target range of $29 to $39 around a $34 base case. The investment case is a genuine cyclical inflection: Q2'26 net sales rose 20% to $12.1 billion, the quarter swung to $802 million of GAAP net income, operating EBITDA more than tripled to $2,312 million from $703 million, and management raised in-year self-help guidance to more than $1.3 billion. That is enough to move the stock off the trough but not enough, in our view, to justify a Buy while two things remain unresolved.

First, the recovery is price-led - prices rose while volume fell 1% - and consensus itself expects FY27E EPS ($1.78) to fall below FY26E ($2.39), so the market is pricing a partial give-back. Second, the dividend still exceeds free cash flow, as it did in FY25. Our probability-weighted value sits above the $28.65 price but below the $34.44 Street target, and our $22 bear case is about 23% lower - a reward that does not clearly outweigh the cyclical risk. We would turn more constructive if free cash flow turns positive and volume, not just price, begins to grow.
